title: Update: I draw the character by hand, the AI only changes what I circle, and now a high-detail 3D model
author: Remarkable_Chip_2717
selftext:
Two days ago I shared my little Mac app, Firstform. Here's an update with a full character I drew myself:

1. I drew her by hand (about 1h20m with my Wacom).  
2. When I want a part changed, I circle only that part with the lasso and say what I want. The rest stays my drawing (the slowed-down part of the video).  
3. It makes front/side/back views of my design, then a 3D model (Tripo), here on the new high-detail setting.  
4. Props like her sword are made separately, so they don't get baked into the body. The model opens in Blender.

Still rough in places: the 3D gave her blue eyes she doesn't have, so I'm working on that. A Windows version is in testing.

Question for character artists: would you use this to block out a character before sculpting? What would make you trust the AI step more?

comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
How would you work with this if you want to make and modify the back view as well? I'm interested. (I draw characters too.)

Like, I enjoy what it made the side/back designs -- but you want to alternate it slightly -- what would be your go-to in this case? Is this process isolated to one-pass front view only?

replies.author: Remarkable_Chip_2717
replies.body:
Not front only! The turnaround comes out as one sheet with all 4 views, and each view is also saved separately. If I like the back but want to change it a bit, I bring the sheet onto the canvas as a layer. Then I either paint over it myself or circle that part with the lasso and describe the change. When it looks right, I save it as the main picture, the app splits it back into the 4 views, and the 3D uses my edited versions.

The honest limit: changing the back doesn't update the other views by itself. So for something that shows from several angles, like a belt or a cape, I fix each view that shows it. Would that work for how you draw?

replies.author: Briskfall
replies.body:
More questions, since you don't seem to mind!

\- Does it work only very well if it's a clean draft, like the one you showed in your trailer? Does it work only effectively if it follows a certain line weight convention? I speedpaint with colours with large strokes a lot -- so I'm wondering if I would need to prepare monochrome linearts for your tool to be digested properly. Some samples of what would turn out to be garbage vs non garbage would be nice.

\- You showed different "parts" (detachable ones) -- and you explained how the different parts can be fit/work. Does it generate a new model every time? And you have to clean up later. I get that for some obvious ones (line the sword) it's generated separately -- but how do you handle ones like the mechanical arms/gauntlets? Is it easier for you for these types of parts, to be built separately or generated all at once? Or is cleaning up the right way?

\- Is the tool built/specialized for humanoid assets and might fail elsewhere? Where and what are the bounds?

I'm not a 3D modeller (though I'm not against picking it up, if the tool requires it), but I've done some 3D sculpting and mainly dabble with 2D concept art. What pipeline do you use, if you don't mind me asking? (I'm asking for reference to see if the barrier isn't too hard to adopt, and if I can integrate it in my workflow)

replies.author: Remarkable_Chip_2717
replies.body:
Great questions!

1. No clean lineart needed. You can upload any picture, including colour speedpaints, and the AI reads shapes and colours, not line weight. The rougher it is, the more it has to guess, so it invents more details. That's why I fix things with the lasso before going 3D. If you want, send me one of your speedpaints and I'll run it through and show you the result, good or garbage 😄

2. For drawing: no, it only regenerates the part I circle, on a new layer, and I merge it if I like it. For 3D: right now it builds the whole model from the 4 views. Big separate props like the sword get their own model. For things like the mechanical arm, I'm planning a tool that splits the model into parts, so you can regenerate only the part that's off. Maybe even a 3D lasso.

3. I started with humanoids because that's what I'm working on, but I want it to work for any asset. The bounds are there for you to find 🤭

Pipeline: I draw in the app, Google's image model does the clean-up and the turnaround views, Tripo builds the 3D.  
You can also run local ai models for drawing and for 3d as well if you pc can handle those heavy things🫣

Honestly, I've mostly tested my own kind of drawing, so I don't have garbage vs non-garbage samples yet. But of course i have some drawings which didn’t looked good and i had to fix it, the same with 3d models. That's why I'd love to try one of yours.

The 3D comes out dense (about 2 million faces), so it needs cleanup or retopology before animation. It's Mac only for now, Windows is in testing, and it uses your own Google and Tripo keys, so each result costs a little.

comments.author: These-Nothing508
comments.body: Is this optimized enough to use in a game?

replies.author: Remarkable_Chip_2717
replies.body:
Not straight away. The detailed model in the video is about 2 million triangles, which is great for looking at or baking, but too heavy for a game. Right now I'd take it into Blender to retopologize and bake the details down. The app already has a "Clean quad" option that asks Tripo for a lighter quad mesh (around 10-25k faces) for game use, but I haven't fully tested it yet. Auto-rigging and a proper game-ready export are on my list next.  
😌

replies.author: These-Nothing508
replies.body:
Hey, first of all, thanks so much for sharing this with me.

I’ve also tried other 3D platforms, like Meshy, Hitem, Hyper3D, etc. The results weren’t great. They either weren’t optimized, or at around 30K polys there were issues in areas like the hands and neck, for example.

Some platforms have rig systems that auto-rig and let you choose animations. Those worked well. Applying animations like walking, fighting, or dancing to the character takes just a few seconds. But finding a good platform that handles everything end to end isn’t really possible.

I dropped a model I made in Hyper3D into my game and used it without any problems. It was around 25K polys, but there were minor visual issues in the tricky areas I mentioned.

Over the past few days I’ve tried all the LLM models: Opus 5.5, Sol 6.1, Gemini Argon. If you let them download textures, these models can do things like houses pretty well. They’re genuinely usable in a game, around 10K polys on average. But they’re not good at complex things like humans or animals. They burn a lot of tokens and still don’t produce a usable asset in return.

They can create rigs and add animations, but again, those aren’t perfect either. For example, when you do a kick motion, it only animates the leg area, so you don’t get a fully realistic full-body animation. If you iterate a lot, maybe you can get something realistic. The animations aren’t high quality, but they’re okay-ish.

So I’m going to focus on more mechanical things in my game. I’ll wait for the next 3D and LLM models. New Claude, GPT, and Gemini models are coming out very soon anyway. But if I wanted to produce something today, I’d probably do what you did with Tripo and then try adding rigging and animation with an LLM and use that.

By the way, before I generate an image, I generate reference images first, with GPT or Gemini. In that reference image I set up the character’s basic, costume-free form. Once I have that physical structure to use as a reference for the mesh, I send it to 3D generation.

My goal is actually to get the character’s body structure first and then add extra costumes, but I haven’t been able to try that yet, because as I said earlier, I haven’t been able to get characters at the level I want.

replies.author: Remarkable_Chip_2717
replies.body:
This is super helpful, thank you! Funny thing: your "body first, then costumes" idea is exactly what I'm thinking about too. My clean-quad test had the same weak spot you describe, with no neck under the scarf, so a body-first step might fix both. Auto-rig + picking animations is on my list as well. If I get the body-first flow working, would you be up for trying it on one of your characters?  
Also which platform auto-rig worked best for you?

replies.author: These-Nothing508
replies.body:
Yes, definitely. I’d be happy to test it on one of my characters.

I looked into platforms that do 3D auto-rigging and animation, but they don’t rig and animate existing 3D models. They generate everything from scratch. I may have given you incomplete information about the animations: they don’t create them from scratch with a prompt. You can pick from pre-made animations in a library. Those weren’t suitable in my case. They also charge for downloads, but if you just want to try it, you can check out [https://hyper3d.ai](https://hyper3d.ai/).

I just tried free rigging and animation on [https://www.mixamo.com](https://www.mixamo.com), and it works pretty well. It might be useful for you, so I’d recommend taking a look. I think once the next LLM models come out, there won’t be any need for extra platforms anyway. I feel like they’ll work directly in Blender and produce quality results themselves, but that’s just a guess.
